name: Illusion of explanatory depth
statement: People rate their understanding of how everyday things work higher than they can demonstrate, and the rating falls once they try to write the explanation out.
meaning: The claim is narrower than it sounds. It is not that people are generally overconfident about what they know. It is that one particular kind of knowledge, the causal mechanism by which something works, invites a confidence that other kinds do not. Rozenblit and Keil's method is three steps: rate your understanding of a zip fastener or a flush toilet on a seven-point scale, write out how it works, then rate yourself again. The gap between the two ratings is the illusion. Their explanation is that a device offers visible parts, a familiar function and a name, and people mistake the availability of those cues for possession of the mechanism. Their Study 12 supports the first of those, with the ratio of visible to hidden parts the best predictor of how far a rating fell.

origin.note: Their paper is "The misunderstood limits of folk science: an illusion of explanatory depth", volume 26, pages 521 to 562. It reports twelve studies and coins the name.

evidence: Study 1 asked 16 Yale graduate students to rate 48 phenomena, 40 distracters and eight test items, most of them taken from a CD-ROM version of The Way Things Work. Ratings came five times: before explaining, after explaining, after a diagnostic question, after reading an expert account, and once more for what the account had just taught them. Time was reliable, F(4, 56) = 16.195, p < .001, eta-squared = .536, and the contrasts from Time 1 to Times 2, 3 and 4 all held at p < .002. Study 2 repeated it on 33 Yale undergraduates, F(4, 124) = 38.9, p < .001, eta-squared = .555, with no interaction between study and time. Study 3 ran the same materials on 16 students at a regional non-selective state campus, F(3, 42) = 23.557, p < .001, eta-squared = .627. Study 5 gave the Study 2 explanations to 12 fresh raters, whose mean judgement of them was 2.72 against self-ratings of 3.89 before explaining and 3.10 after. Study 6 warned 31 undergraduates in advance that they would be tested, which shrank the fall without removing it. Studies 7 to 10 swapped the material, testing 52 people on capital cities, 37 on procedures, 39 on film plots and 31 on natural phenomena, against a devices group of 97 pooled from Studies 1 to 4. Table 7 gives the average Time 1 minus Time 2 drop by domain: .918 for devices, .860 for natural phenomena such as tides and rainbows, .351 for the plots of popular films, .291 for the capital cities of countries and minus .173 for procedures such as baking chocolate chip cookies. The rise for procedures did not reach significance, F(2, 70) = 1.598, p = .210.

replication.headline: The rating drop repeats wherever it is tried. The political version of the finding, which is the one that made the idea famous, has failed or reversed more often than it has held.
replication.detail: Two bodies of evidence, and they point different ways. The basic illusion holds. Alter, Oppenheimer and Zemla tested 100 adults and kept 60 after an instructional check, and rated understanding of three devices fell 0.42 points, t(58) = 3.89, p < .0001. Gaviria and Corredor recruited 262 Colombian students and analysed 255, finding a fall of 0.99 points on national historical events, 95% CI [0.80, 1.17], t(254) = 10.51, d = 0.66. Meyers, Gretton, Budge, Fugelsang and Koehler ran three preregistered experiments on 240, 327 and 264 people recruited from Mechanical Turk and found the fall even for phenomena the participant had not been asked to explain. The political application is the contested one. Fernbach, Rogers, Fox and Sloman asked people to explain policies such as a single-payer health system or a carbon cap-and-trade scheme. Their Experiment 1 measured understanding on all 198 participants, 3.82 before and 3.45 after, F(1, 197) = 34.69, p < .001. The moderation result rests on the 87 who also rated their position beforehand, whose extremity fell from 1.41 to 1.28 on a scale running 0 to 3, F(1, 86) = 6.10, p = .016, partial eta-squared = .066. Crawford and Ruscio ran two preregistered close replications of that paper's Experiment 2, on 306 and 405 people, and a close and conceptual replication of its Experiment 3 on 343. None of the key effects reached significance, one survived a small-telescopes analysis, and reported understanding still fell. Walker, Zhang and Cheng report three replications on 5,139 citizens in Hong Kong and positional extremity higher, not lower, after citizens articulated their understanding. Sloman and Vives recruited 739 people on Prolific and recovered the moderation effect in the 305-strong explanation condition, but only for policies framed around consequences, t(304) = 3.03, p = .002, with no change for policies resting on protected values, t(304) = 0.06, p = .95. Two recent preregistered efforts test the intervention rather than the effect. Knöchelmann, Janssen, Dörbaum, Heck and Cohrs put an explanatory-depth arm into an intervention tournament on 1,503 people, and what raised intellectual humility about political topics was a text about the benefits of humility. Elnakouri, Huynh and Grossmann report across five experiments, three of them preregistered, that explaining a contentious political issue made thinking more open-minded rather than more entrenched.

study.cite: Crawford, J. T., & Ruscio, J. (2021). Asking people to explain complex policies does not increase political moderation: Three preregistered failures to closely replicate Fernbach, Rogers, Fox, and Sloman's (2013) findings. Psychological Science, 32(4), 611-621.

limits: Rozenblit and Keil's samples are small, 16 graduate students in Study 1 and 33 undergraduates in Study 2, though Study 3 answered the charge of Ivy League overconfidence by running 16 students at a regional non-selective campus. The measure is a change in self-rating rather than a test of knowledge, which is what Study 5 was for: independent raters scored the explanations lower than the writers had scored themselves beforehand. Ratings do not bounce back to where they started. The paper reports no change from Time 3 to Time 4, and the rise at Time 5 is a rating of the knowledge the expert account had just supplied. The illusion is domain-bound by the authors' own data, absent for procedures and film plots. Later work narrows it further. Alter, Oppenheimer and Zemla shrank it by inducing a concrete construal style. Meyers and colleagues found the fall for phenomena nobody had explained, and in their third experiment people who copied out a block of descriptive text also fell, t(144) = -3.62, though explainers fell further, t(195.43) = -2.85, p = .002. That paper reports one-tailed tests throughout. Andrew Zeveney's Lehigh master's thesis, supervised by Jessecae Marsh, put 251 Mechanical Turk workers across five domains and found a time by domain interaction, F(4, 237) = 4.79, p = .001, with the fall holding for devices, mental disorders and both treatment domains and absent for medical disorders. A second experiment on 100 people found the fall after explaining and not after describing, F(1, 96) = 11.71, p = .001, and a third on 101 people found no fall among those told that scientists understand mental health poorly, F(1, 97) = 6.05, p = .016. That thesis is not peer reviewed. Crawford and Ruscio's article was not obtained. It is closed at Sage, Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no free copy, and Ruscio's own publications page at tcnj.edu returned 403 to this session on 17 August 2026, so the sample sizes and conclusions quoted here come from the abstract at PubMed. Walker, Zhang and Cheng is closed too, and only the abstract deposited at Crossref is used; 5,139 is their total across three studies and no per-study figure is quoted here.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating the two evidence bases as one. That people overrate their grasp of a zip fastener is well supported and repeatedly reproduced. That asking a voter to explain a policy makes their politics more moderate is a separate claim from a separate paper, and preregistered replication has gone against it. The first does not vouch for the second. A second error is reading the rating drop as a measure of ignorance about the thing explained. It measures how far a self-rating moves, and Meyers and colleagues watched it move for phenomena the participant was never asked to explain. A third is treating the effect as general overconfidence. Rozenblit and Keil built four studies to rule that out, and the drop for capital cities was .291 against .918 for devices. Overconfidence in the wider sense is entry 77, the Dunning-Kruger effect is entry 4, and the curse of knowledge, which runs the other way, is entry 28. The argument from incredulity, entry 490, is the opposite move again, an inference drawn from failing to imagine a mechanism rather than confidence in one. On the political dispute, the two sides agree about the first step: Crawford and Ruscio and Sloman and Vives both report reported understanding falling in their own data while the attitude change did not follow, and that split is what the argument is about.
